title: Representation, perspective and voice
summary: Texts never simply mirror reality: they select, frame and construct it. Learn to analyse whose perspective is shown, whose is missing, and how voice shapes our response.

keyterms.definition: The way a text constructs an image of people, places, groups or ideas through selection and framing; one of the course's seven key concepts.
The point of view or set of values from which a text presents its subject; a key concept of the course.
The distinctive personality, attitude and style of a speaker or narrator as heard through the language.
A one-sided presentation that favours one view, often through selection, omission or loaded language.
An oversimplified, generalised representation of a group, often reinforcing prejudice.
How a text selects and emphasises aspects of an issue to guide interpretation, e.g. a headline framing protest as 'chaos'.
What a text leaves out; absences can be as revealing as what is shown.
A constructed speaking identity adopted by a writer, such as the 'I' in a poem or a brand's voice.
Words with strong emotional connotations used to influence the reader's attitude.
A perspective that is pushed to the edges or excluded by dominant texts and discourses.

questions.prompt: Headline A: "Youths rampage through city centre." Headline B: "Students march for climate action." What does the contrast best show?
options: The same event can be represented very differently through word choice
questions.explanation: 'Youths rampage' frames the group as threatening; 'students march' frames them as purposeful citizens.

questions.statement: A documentary photograph is a neutral, unmediated record of reality.
questions.explanation: Photographers select subject, angle, moment and crop, and editors choose captions. All of these construct a representation.

questions.text: An oversimplified, generalised image of a group is a ___.
questions.explanation: Analysing stereotypes means asking what they simplify and whom they serve.

questions.prompt: An article on a factory closure quotes three managers but no workers. What should an analyst note?
questions.explanation: Whose voices are included and excluded is a key part of how a text represents an issue.

questions.prompt: Match the word to how it frames a person who crosses a border.
questions.explanation: Labels carry connotations that frame identity and invite particular judgements.

questions.prompt: "Bureaucrats in Brussels have once again meddled in our affairs." Which words are most loaded?
questions.explanation: 'Bureaucrats' connotes faceless red tape and 'meddled' connotes unwelcome interference; together they create hostility.

questions.statement: Bias can be created by selection and placement of information, not only by opinionated words.
questions.explanation: Putting one side first, giving it more space or omitting counter-evidence can all create bias in apparently neutral language.

questions.text: How a text selects and emphasises aspects of an issue to guide interpretation is called ___.
questions.explanation: Framing works through headlines, images, order and vocabulary.

questions.prompt: Which question best probes representation in an advert for a family car?
options: How many words does it use?
What kind of family is shown, and who is left out?
What font size is used for the price?
questions.explanation: Asking who is shown, how, and who is absent reveals the ideals and assumptions the advert constructs.

questions.prompt: Order these questions for analysing representation.
items: Who or what is being represented?
What are the effects and implications?
questions.explanation: Moving from subject to method to perspective to consequences builds a critical reading.

lessons.title: Voice, persona and point of view

questions.prompt: A clothing brand tweets: "ngl our new hoodies are kinda iconic 🔥". What has the brand created?
questions.explanation: Slang, abbreviation and emoji construct a casual, peer-like persona to make the brand feel like a friend.

questions.text: A constructed speaking identity adopted by a writer is a ___.
questions.explanation: The speaker of a poem or the 'I' of a column is a persona, not simply the writer themselves.

questions.statement: The speaker of a first-person poem should always be assumed to be the poet.
questions.explanation: Poets often adopt personas, so refer to 'the speaker' unless the text is clearly autobiographical.

questions.prompt: A short story is told by a grieving teenager who keeps changing the subject. What does this voice most likely suggest?
options: She is avoiding pain she cannot yet face
The story is a news report
questions.explanation: Deflection and evasion in a narrating voice can reveal emotion indirectly.

questions.prompt: Match the concept to the question it answers.

pairs.right: From whose viewpoint is this seen?
What is emphasised to guide us?

questions.explanation: These concepts overlap but each opens a different line of analysis.

questions.prompt: Why might a novelist tell a story from the viewpoint of a domestic worker in a wealthy household?
options: To give voice to a marginalised perspective and expose the family from below
questions.explanation: Shifting perspective to someone usually unheard can critique power and privilege.

questions.statement: Texts can challenge stereotypes as well as reinforce them.
questions.explanation: Writers may subvert expectations to expose and question stereotypes; analyse which a text does.

questions.text: A one-sided presentation that favours a particular view shows ___.
questions.explanation: Identify how bias is produced: word choice, selection, omission or structure.

questions.prompt: An infographic about a city uses only photos of glass towers and luxury restaurants. What is the clearest effect?
options: It represents the city as uniformly wealthy and modern, omitting other realities
It focuses on the city's history
It targets the city's poorest residents
questions.explanation: Selective imagery constructs an aspirational representation, likely for investors or tourists.

questions.prompt: Order these phrases from most neutral to most loaded.
items: The council scrapped the policy without warning
The council betrayed residents by axing the policy
questions.explanation: Verbs like 'scrapped' and 'axing' and accusations like 'betrayed' progressively add judgement.
